documents.title: Text of Infection Control and Epidemiology

chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION Ankle fractures, common yet significant injuries in orthopaedic practice, have seen a rising trend in incidence, primarily attributed to an aging population and increased sports‐related activities. , This escalation necessitates a deeper exploration into the outcomes and complications associated with ankle fracture fixation, particularly postoperative surgical site infections (SSIs), which remain a major concern in orthopaedic surgeries. SSIs not only pose immediate health risks but also have far‐reaching implications on patient recovery and healthcare systems. , These include severe pain at the infection site, marked swelling and redness, which may rapidly escalate to systemic symptoms like fever, chills and tachycardia. In some cases, these infections can lead to acute septicemia, a life‐threatening condition that requires prompt medical intervention. Early onset of SSIs often necessitates urgent surgical debridement, prolonged antibiotic therapy and, in some cases, may even necessitate the removal of the surgical fixation device to control the infection. The anatomical complexity of the ankle, comprising the distal ends of the tibia and fibula, and the talus, renders it especially susceptible to postoperative complications. The limited soft tissue coverage around the ankle joint further increases the risk of SSIs. Among the various complications associated with ankle fracture fixation, the most common include delayed union or non‐union of the fracture, malalignment and nerve or blood vessel damage. However, postoperative SSIs are not only common but also represent one of the most severe complications due to their potential to significantly worsen patient outcomes. SSIs often led to prolonged hospitalization, additional surgical interventions and, in severe cases, may result in chronic osteomyelitis or amputation. Furthermore, SSIs following ankle fracture fixation can compromise the integrity of the fixation device, thereby jeopardizing the overall success of the surgical procedure. , These infections can manifest in various forms, ranging from superficial incisional SSIs to deep, more severe infections involving the bone and joint structures. Superficial incisional SSIs involve only the skin and subcutaneous tissue and are often characterized by redness, swelling and pain at the incision site. These infections are generally more manageable with local wound care and oral antibiotics. Deep incisional SSIs extend into the deep soft tissues, such as fascial and muscle layers. They can present with discharge, dehiscence or abscess formation and often require more aggressive interventions, including intravenous antibiotics and surgical debridement. The most severe category, organ/space SSIs, involves structures deeper than the fascial/muscle layers, including the joint or bone. These infections, such as osteomyelitis or septic arthritis, are the most challenging to treat, requiring prolonged antimicrobial therapy and potentially multiple surgical interventions. The severity of SSIs can escalate to osteomyelitis or joint sepsis, which are challenging to treat and often require long‐term medical intervention. The consequences of SSIs extend beyond the physical to encompass significant psychological and economic impacts. Patients suffering from SSIs experience prolonged hospital stays, repeated surgeries and often prolonged courses of antibiotic therapy, leading to increased healthcare costs. Moreover, the psychological impact on patients, including anxiety and depression due to prolonged recovery periods, is an area of growing concern. This situation underscores the need for a comprehensive understanding of the risk factors associated with SSIs in ankle fracture fixation to develop targeted prevention and management strategies. The aetiology of SSIs in the context of ankle fractures is multifactorial, encompassing patient‐specific factors, surgical techniques and postoperative care. Patient‐specific risk factors include, but are not limited to, diabetes mellitus, smoking, obesity, peripheral vascular disease and immunocompromised states. These conditions can impair wound healing and increase susceptibility to infection. Surgical factors, such as the duration and complexity of the procedure, use of different fixation devices and the skill level of the surgical team, also significantly influence SSI risk. The postoperative period is critical for infection prevention, with factors like wound care, antibiotic prophylaxis and patient education playing pivotal roles. The purpose of this systematic review and meta‐analysis is to comprehensively evaluate the risk factors associated with the development of SSIs in patients undergoing ankle fracture fixation. By systematically reviewing the existing literature and analysing data from multiple studies, this research aims to identify and quantify the key risk factors. 2 MATERIALS AND METHODS 2.1 Search strategy In conducting this systematic review and meta‐analysis, our methodology was rigorously aligned with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Our meta‐analytical framework was systematically structured around the PICO model, which encompasses: Patient Population (P), referring to individuals subjected to surgical fixation post‐ankle fractures; Intervention (I), which in this context is the ankle fracture surgical fixation procedure itself; Comparison (C), involving a thorough investigation and analysis of a variety of risk factors and their correlation with the incidence of postoperative surgical site infections (SSIs); and Outcome (O), focused on the frequency of SSIs consequent to ankle fracture surgical fixation, alongside an examination of the myriad risk factors that precipitate these

Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Our meta‐analytical framework was systematically structured around the PICO model, which encompasses: Patient Population (P), referring to individuals subjected to surgical fixation post‐ankle fractures; Intervention (I), which in this context is the ankle fracture surgical fixation procedure itself; Comparison (C), involving a thorough investigation and analysis of a variety of risk factors and their correlation with the incidence of postoperative surgical site infections (SSIs); and Outcome (O), focused on the frequency of SSIs consequent to ankle fracture surgical fixation, alongside an examination of the myriad risk factors that precipitate these complications. A comprehensive literature search was executed across four major electronic databases: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, on September 26, 2023. This search, transcending temporal boundaries, incorporated a meticulously crafted strategy deploying keywords such as “ankle fracture,” “surgical fixation,” “surgical site infection,” “ssi,” “risk factors,” and “postoperative complications.” These terms were meticulously chosen to reflect the extensive spectrum of the PICO framework and to guarantee an exhaustive collation of pertinent studies for our meta‐analysis. No restrictions were imposed based on language. Additionally, the reference lists of relevant articles were meticulously scanned to identify any further potential sources. 2.2 Inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria 2.2.1 Inclusion criteria Study Design: Peer‐reviewed studies including randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, case–control studies and observational studies examining the risk factors for surgical site infections (SSIs) post‐ankle fracture fixation. Participants: Studies involving patients of any age who have undergone surgical fixation for ankle fractures. Outcomes: Studies must report on the incidence of SSIs following ankle fracture fixation, with clear definitions and diagnostic criteria for SSIs. Risk Factors: Studies that specifically investigate risk factors contributing to the development of SSIs post‐ankle fracture fixation. Language: Studies published in any language, provided there is an English abstract available. 2.2.2 Exclusion criteria Non‐Relevant Study Designs: Editorials, letters, conference abstracts, case reports and reviews without original data. Non‐Specific Patient Population: Studies focusing on patients undergoing surgeries other than ankle fracture fixation or studies where the data specific to ankle fracture fixation cannot be isolated. Non‐Specific Outcomes: Studies that do not specifically report on SSIs as an outcome or lack clear diagnostic criteria for SSIs. Incomplete Data: Studies with incomplete data or insufficient detail regarding the methodology or results. Duplicate Publications: Studies that are duplicate publications or sub‐studies of already included articles. 2.3 Data extraction In the meta‐analysis, literature screening and data extraction were conducted independently by two researchers and subsequently cross‐validated to ensure accuracy and consistency. Should any discrepancies arise during this process, the reviewers engaged in a discussion to reach a consensus, resorting to consultation with a third‐party evaluator when necessary. Extracted data encompassed various parameters including the authorship of each study, publication year, the sample size, country of origin, type of study, duration of follow‐up and key risk factors identified. In instances where relevant data were not discernible in the published reports, efforts were made to contact the original study investigators via email to obtain the unpublished data, thereby ensuring a comprehensive dataset for analysis. 2.4 Quality assessment In conducting our meta‐analysis, the methodological quality of each included study was evaluated independently by two reviewers utilizing the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale (NOS). This scale, recognized for its robustness, assigns a score to each study based on a comprehensive assessment of nine criteria distributed across three key domains: selection, comparability and outcome, thereby facilitating a thorough evaluation of potential biases within the studies. Upon completing this detailed assessment, studies were scored on a scale ranging from 0 to 9. The quality scores were interpreted as follows: studies with scores from 0 to 3 were categorized as low quality, scores between 4 and 6 indicated moderate quality studies and scores from 7 to 9 were indicative of high‐quality research. 2.5 Statistical analyses In our meta‐analysis, the statistical analyses were conducted with a focus on assessing heterogeneity between studies. This assessment was performed using chi‐square statistics, and the degree of heterogeneity was quantified using the I 2 statistic. When the I 2 value was observed to be <50% accompanied by a p ‐value equal to or >0.10, it was inferred that there was no significant heterogeneity among the studies. Under these circumstances, a fixed‐effects model was applied for the computation of the combined effect size. Conversely, significant heterogeneity was indicated when the I 2 value reached or exceeded 50%, or when the corresponding p ‐value was <0.10. In scenarios characterized by such statistical heterogeneity, the random‐effects model was utilized to calculate the aggregated effect size. Sensitivity analysis played a crucial role in our statistical methodology. It was conducted to assess the stability of our findings and to identify any potential sources of heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis played a crucial role in our statistical methodology. It was conducted to assess the stability of our findings and to identify any potential sources of heterogeneity. This involved a sequential exclusion of each study from the meta‐analysis, followed by a recalculation of the overall effect size, thereby evaluating the influence of individual studies on the cumulative findings. To investigate the presence of potential publication bias, we analysed the symmetry of the funnel plot. An evenly distributed pattern of data points on both sides of the apex of the funnel plot would suggest a reduced likelihood of results being skewed by publication bias. Furthermore, Egger's linear regression test was employed as a quantitative tool to detect any indications of publication bias. All statistical tests in our analysis were two‐sided. A p ‐value of <0.05 was considered to denote statistical significance. For the purpose of these analyses, Stata version 17 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA) was utilized. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Search results and study selection During the initial phase of our systematic review and meta‐analysis, a thorough search across multiple electronic databases yielded a preliminary collection of 1250 articles deemed potentially relevant. To streamline this pool, a systematic approach was adopted to eliminate duplicate entries, ensuring the representation of each unique study only once. Following this, titles and abstracts of these articles were meticulously screened against a set of predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. These criteria were comprehensive, encompassing aspects such as study design, demographic characteristics of the participants, measured clinical outcomes and the overall methodological quality of the studies. This initial screening process led to the selection of 34 articles for a more detailed examination. Each of these articles underwent an in‐depth full‐text review conducted independently by multiple investigators, adhering to an objective and thorough evaluation protocol. During this intensive review phase, 27 articles were excluded due to specific reasons, categorized as follows: review articles ( n = 7), sequentially published studies ( n = 7), studies with inadequate data for meaningful analysis ( n = 7) and clinical trials without control groups ( n = 6). Consequently, after this rigorous selection process, a total of 7 articles were identified as fulfilling all the strict criteria outlined in our research methodology. , , , , , , These articles were thus incorporated into the final meta‐analysis. The process of study selection and the number of articles included at each stage of the review are illustrated in Figure . 3.2 Study characteristics In the meta‐analysis, the characteristics of the included studies were diverse yet systematic. The studies, conducted between 2006 and 2019, were predominantly case–control in design, with a few cohort studies included to enrich the analysis. The sample sizes varied, ranging from as few as 13 participants in the control group to as many as 2543, indicating a broad spectrum of study scales. Geographically, the studies spanned multiple countries, with a notable concentration in China, reflecting the global interest and relevance of the topic. Other countries represented included Japan, Norway, Finland and the United Kingdom, contributing to the international scope of the analysis. The follow‐up periods of these studies also varied, ranging from a year to several years, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of the outcomes over different time frames. This variation in follow‐up periods provided valuable insights into both short‐term and long‐term effects within the respective study scopes (Table ). 3.3 Results of quality assessment The results of this quality assessment revealed that most studies achieved high scores, reflecting their overall methodological robustness. The total scores ranged from 7 to 9 out of a possible 9 points, indicating a generally high quality of the included studies. Each study demonstrated strong representativeness of the exposed cohort and appropriate selection of the non‐exposed cohort. The ascertainment of exposure and the adequacy of follow‐up were also well addressed in most studies. Furthermore, the comparability of cohorts based on design or analysis and the assessment of outcomes were also satisfactorily reported in the majority of the studies. This comprehensive quality assessment underscores the reliability and validity of the findings derived from these studies. Overall, the high‐quality scores across the studies suggest a strong methodological foundation for the meta‐analysis, providing confidence in the robustness and credibility of its conclusions (Table ). 3.4 Impact of diabetes on postoperative surgical site infections In this meta‐analysis, a focused examination was conducted on the relationship between diabetes and the incidence of postoperative SSIs. Overall, the high‐quality scores across the studies suggest a strong methodological foundation for the meta‐analysis, providing confidence in the robustness and credibility of its conclusions (Table ). 3.4 Impact of diabetes on postoperative surgical site infections In this meta‐analysis, a focused examination was conducted on the relationship between diabetes and the incidence of postoperative SSIs. Out of the studies analysed, six specifically investigated the impact of diabetes on the occurrence of SSIs. A key component of our analysis involved assessing the heterogeneity across these studies. The heterogeneity analysis revealed no significant variability among the study results, as indicated by an I 2 value of 0.0% and a p ‐value of 0.785. The meta‐analysis results underscored a significant association between diabetes and an increased risk of postoperative infections. The pooled odds ratio (OR) was found to be 1.65, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 1.16 to 2.34. This OR reflects a 65% increase in the risk of developing SSIs in diabetic patients compared to non‐diabetic patients (Figure ). 3.5 Influence of smoking on postoperative surgical site infections This segment of the meta‐analysis delved into the impact of smoking on the incidence of postoperative SSIs. The analysis was based on six studies that specifically investigated the relationship between smoking and postoperative SSIs. A critical aspect of this analysis was the assessment of heterogeneity among the included studies. The heterogeneity analysis revealed a considerable variation, as evidenced by an I 2 value of 63.8% and a p ‐value of 0.017. This substantial heterogeneity necessitated the use of a random‐effects model for the meta‐analysis, which is more appropriate in accounting for variability among studies. The meta‐analysis results demonstrated a significant correlation between smoking and an increased risk of developing postoperative infections. The calculated pooled OR for smokers versus non‐smokers was 1.79, with a 95% CI of 1.41–2.27. This OR indicates that smokers have a 79% higher risk of postoperative SSIs compared with non‐smokers (Figure ). 3.6 Association between open fractures and postoperative surgical site infections The heterogeneity analysis yielded an I 2 value of 55.3% and a p ‐value of 0.107. Although this I 2 value suggests moderate heterogeneity, the p ‐value indicates a lack of statistically significant variability among the study results. The meta‐analysis results revealed a substantial increase in the risk of postoperative SSIs associated with open fractures. The pooled OR was 4.87, with a 95% CI ranging from 3.2 to 7.41. This OR indicates that patients with open fractures have an almost fivefold increased risk of developing postoperative SSIs compared with those without open fractures (Figure ). 3.7 Analysis of risk factors for surgical site infections in ankle fracture patients The analysis revealed that age significantly influences the risk of SSIs in patients with ankle fractures. With a fixed‐effects model due to low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 23.4%, p = 0.207), the combined effect showed an OR of 4.65, indicating a marked increase in infection risk with advancing age. This finding, with a 95% CI of 3.06–6.31 and a highly significant p ‐value (<0.001), underscores the necessity for heightened surveillance and tailored postoperative care in older patients. Alcohol consumption was identified as another significant risk factor. The fixed‐effects model analysis, justified by a low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 5%), showed an OR of 1.57. This suggests that patients with a history of alcohol consumption have a 57% higher risk of developing SSIs. The 95% CI ranged from 1.20 to 2.08, and the statistical significance was evident ( p < 0.01). This result emphasizes the importance of preoperative screening and counselling on alcohol consumption. Patients with an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score of 3 or higher also exhibited a significantly higher risk of SSIs. The fixed model, chosen due to negligible heterogeneity ( I 2 = 1.8%, p = 0.369), revealed an OR of 2.07. This indicates that patients with a higher ASA score, reflecting poorer general health status, are more than twice as likely to develop SSIs. BMI also appeared as a significant risk factor. With an OR of 0.84 and a 95% CI of 0.37–1.31 ( p < 0.001), the analysis using a fixed model (due to moderate heterogeneity, I 2 = 36%) suggests that higher BMI is associated with an increased risk of SSIs. This finding calls for targeted strategies to manage and monitor patients with higher BMI undergoing ankle fracture surgery. This finding calls for targeted strategies to manage and monitor patients with higher BMI undergoing ankle fracture surgery. The presence of a contaminated incision significantly raised the risk of SSIs, as evidenced by an OR of 4.63 in a random‐effects model ( I 2 = 51.3%, p = 0.036). This high risk, with a 95% CI of 2.94–7.38, indicates the critical need for strict aseptic techniques and infection control measures in surgeries involving contaminated incisions. Fracture dislocation was another identified risk factor, with an OR of 1.74 (95% CI: 1.36–2.20, p < 0.01) in a fixed‐effects model. The lack of heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%) strengthens the reliability of this finding, suggesting that dislocated fractures are more prone to postoperative infections. Lastly, the presence of heart disease was found to significantly increase the risk of SSIs. The fixed‐effects model analysis, with no heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%, p = 0.702), showed an OR of 2.97. This denotes those patients with heart disease are almost three times more likely to develop SSIs (95% CI: 1.75–4.98, p < 0.001), highlighting the need for comprehensive cardiovascular assessment and management in these patients (Table ). 3.8 Assessment of publication bias Publication bias was evaluated in this meta‐analysis using funnel plots and Egger's linear regression test. The funnel plots displayed symmetry, suggesting an absence of significant publication bias (Figure ). Additionally, Egger's test results across various variables showed no significant publication bias ( p > 0.05 for all). These findings affirm the robustness and reliability of the meta‐analysis results, indicating that they are not skewed by publication bias. 4 DISCUSSION Ankle fractures are a prevalent injury, especially in the elderly and individuals engaged in physical activities, and represent a significant portion of orthopaedic trauma cases. The management of ankle fractures has evolved substantially, with surgical intervention becoming a cornerstone for ensuring optimal outcomes, particularly in cases involving displacement or instability. , Surgical treatments, ranging from open reduction and internal fixation to more complex reconstructive surgeries, aim to restore the ankle's stability, alignment and functionality. However, the occurrence of SSIs postoperatively presents a major challenge in the management of ankle fractures. SSIs not only delay wound healing and recovery but also increase the risk of complications such as osteomyelitis, chronic pain and even the necessity for additional surgeries. The presence of an SSI can significantly prolong hospital stays, elevate healthcare costs and adversely affect the patient's quality of life. , In severe cases, SSIs can lead to long‐term disability, emphasizing the need for meticulous surgical techniques and postoperative care. Understanding the risk factors and implementing strategies to mitigate SSIs is crucial in the context of ankle fracture management. The negative impact of SSIs on treatment outcomes necessitates a proactive approach, encompassing both preoperative optimization of patient health and rigorous intraoperative infection control measures. This meta‐analysis has identified several critical risk factors for the development of postoperative SSIs in patients, highlighting the complexity of postoperative care. These factors include diabetes, open fractures, smoking, age, alcohol consumption, an ASA score of 3 or higher, higher BMI, the presence of a contaminated incision, fracture dislocation and heart disease. Each of these factors contributes to the heightened risk of SSIs in distinct ways. The strong association of diabetes and open fractures with SSIs underscores the significant challenges in managing patients with these conditions. Diabetes, known for its impact on wound healing due to impaired immune response and reduced blood flow, markedly increases infection risk. Similarly, open fractures, which inherently expose the wound to external contaminants, create an ideal environment for infection. Smoking, age and alcohol consumption were also identified as significant risk factors. Smoking impairs tissue oxygenation and healing, while aging is often associated with diminished physiological reserves and comorbidities, both of which can compromise postoperative recovery. Alcohol consumption can impair immune function and wound healing, further increasing SSI risk. An elevated ASA score indicates more severe systemic disease, which can compromise a patient's ability to recover from surgery and resist infection. Higher BMI has been linked to increased surgical wound complications, possibly due to reduced tissue perfusion and alterations in immune response. Contaminated incisions, by their very nature, carry a high risk of infection, necessitating meticulous surgical technique and postoperative care. The presence of fracture dislocation and heart disease further complicates the postoperative course. Fracture dislocation often results in more extensive surgery, increasing infection risk, while heart disease can limit a patient's physiological capacity to cope with the stress of surgery and infection. The identification of these risk factors provides crucial insights for clinicians. It emphasizes the need for comprehensive preoperative assessments and the development of individualized care plans to mitigate these risks. For high‐risk patients, strategies like stringent glycaemic control, smoking cessation programs, careful wound management and tailored antibiotic prophylaxis should be considered. Moreover, these findings highlight the importance of multidisciplinary approaches involving surgeons, anaesthesiologists, endocrinologists and nursing staff to optimize patient outcomes. Future research should focus on developing and testing targeted interventions to reduce the incidence of SSIs in patients with these identified risk factors. Such studies could significantly contribute to improving surgical outcomes and patient quality of life while reducing healthcare costs associated with SSIs. This study's limitations include considerable heterogeneity in the methodologies and patient demographics of the included research, which might impact the uniformity and applicability of the results. Furthermore, the exclusion of studies published in languages other than English could lead to the omission of pertinent data, potentially affecting the comprehensive nature of the analysis. Additionally, the predominance of observational studies in the dataset restricts the establishment of causality, as these study types are more prone to confounding variables. In the discussion of our findings, it is crucial to acknowledge the implications of the predominance of observational studies in our dataset. Such studies are instrumental for identifying associations but are inherently limited in their ability to establish causal relationships, especially when compared with RCTs. This limitation mainly stems from the absence of randomization in participant selection and potential biases in data collection and analysis. Therefore, while our findings contribute significantly to understanding the risk factors for SSIs post‐ankle fracture fixation, they should be interpreted with caution. These factors collectively necessitate a careful interpretation of the study's conclusions. To overcome these limitations and strengthen future research in this field, we propose several methodological enhancements. Primarily, there is a need for more RCTs, which offer more robust evidence of causality. Advanced statistical methods like propensity score matching and multivariable regression analysis could also enhance the analysis of observational data. Furthermore, longitudinal studies would provide valuable insights into the temporal dynamics of SSIs and their risk factors. Additionally, more detailed reporting of patient demographics, clinical interventions and outcomes in observational studies would facilitate finer adjustments for confounders. Lastly, future meta‐analyses should strive to include a higher proportion of RCTs, thereby yielding a more balanced and comprehensive view of the available evidence. 5 CONCLUSIONS This study identifies diabetes, open fractures, smoking, advanced age, alcohol consumption, ASA score ≥3, high BMI, contaminated incisions, fracture dislocation and heart disease as significant risk factors for postoperative SSIs. Addressing these factors through targeted interventions is crucial for high‐risk patient groups. By implementing specific preventive and management strategies tailored to these risk factors, the incidence of SSIs can be effectively reduced, thereby improving patient outcomes and minimizing the impact of these infections on the healthcare system.
